description: Governs who is allowed to access systems and data and under what conditions. This is the family most organizations spend the most implementation effort on, since it touches account provisioning, least privilege, session limits, and remote access.

Requires role-based security and privacy training so that people understand and follow the policies that technical controls alone can't enforce. It's the smallest family by control count but underpins every other family, since untrained staff routinely defeat well-designed technical controls.
Covers what gets logged, how logs are protected and retained, and how they're reviewed. Strong audit controls are what make incident investigation and non-repudiation possible after the fact.
Deals with formally assessing whether controls work as intended, authorizing a system to operate, and continuously monitoring it afterward rather than treating security as a one-time checkbox.

Establishes baseline configurations, controls how changes are made, and requires a complete inventory of hardware, software, and firmware. Configuration drift is one of the most common root causes of real-world breaches, which is why this family exists.

Addresses how the organization keeps operating, or recovers quickly, after a disruption -- covering backup strategy, alternate processing sites, and recovery testing rather than just having a plan on paper.
Governs how users, devices, and processes prove who they are before being granted access, including password policy, multi-factor authentication, and cryptographic identity verification.

Requires organizations to have a tested plan for detecting, reporting, containing, and recovering from security incidents, plus coordination procedures with outside parties such as law enforcement or regulators.
Covers routine system maintenance activities -- including remote maintenance -- so that upkeep work doesn't itself become a security gap, for example through unmonitored remote maintenance sessions.
Governs how physical and digital media (drives, backup tapes, removable storage) are marked, stored, transported, and ultimately sanitized or destroyed so that decommissioned media doesn't leak data.

Addresses physical facility security: access control to buildings and server rooms, visitor management, and environmental safeguards like fire suppression and power redundancy. Any organization running its own data center implements this family heavily.

Requires organizations to actually document security and privacy plans for each system, including rules of behavior for users and system security architecture, rather than relying on informal or undocumented practices.

Operates at the organization level rather than the system level, covering things like an overall security program plan, a named senior accountable official, and an enterprise-wide risk strategy that individual system owners plug into.
Covers the security-relevant parts of the employee lifecycle: pre-employment screening, access agreements, and prompt access revocation on termination or role transfer.

Added in Revision 5, this family sets requirements for handling personally identifiable information: what authority is needed to process it, how consent and purpose are documented, and how data minimization is applied.

Requires organizations to identify risks, categorize system impact level, and run vulnerability scanning, forming the basis for deciding which control baseline (Low, Moderate, or High) applies to a given system.
Addresses security throughout the system development lifecycle and when acquiring third-party systems or services, including secure development practices and evaluation of vendor security posture.

The largest family by control count, covering encryption, network boundary protection, segmentation, and cryptographic key management -- essentially the technical backbone of network and data-in-transit security.
Focuses on keeping systems and data trustworthy over time: timely patching of known flaws, malicious code protection, and monitoring for unauthorized changes to software or firmware.

Added in Revision 5, this family addresses risk introduced through vendors, suppliers, and third-party components -- including provenance tracking and authenticity verification of acquired hardware and software.
